blocks.text: A **bank account** lets the holder deposit and safeguard money, earn interest and make payments by cheque. The terms below describe the main kinds of deposit and the paperwork around them.

blocks.title: Deposit terms
rows: An arrangement that lets the account holder deposit and safeguard money, earn interest and pay by cheque.
Money that can be withdrawn at any time without advance notice.
A deposit from which the investor cannot withdraw before a fixed period has elapsed. The lock-in period of a term deposit means premature withdrawal is not possible.
An account that has no minimum or average balance requirement, unlike most ordinary accounts.
The amount that must stay in an account to qualify for special services or to avoid a service charge.
A negotiable instrument issued by a bank in return for funds deposited with it, usually carrying interest.
From a banking view, a contract that guarantees income or returns in exchange for a large sum paid either as a lump sum or through periodic payments.
Deposits protected against loss from a bank failure by a deposit insurance body (in the US it is the FDIC; in India the equivalent is the DICGC).
An itemised note of the cash and other funds a customer hands over to the bank for credit to his or her account.
A payment deposited electronically into a person's account at a depository institution.
A card signed by each depositor, used as a means of identification. It represents a contract between the bank and the depositor.
A bank service in which securities and valuables are kept protected in the bank's vaults for customers.

blocks.title: Lock-in means no premature withdrawal
blocks.text: In a term (time) deposit, the **lock-in period** is the span during which you cannot withdraw early. It does not mean that lockers are unavailable or that you cannot open another account.

blocks.title: Demand vs Time deposits
blocks.phrase: Demand = 'Dip in any time'; Time = 'Tied until the time is up'.
letters: Withdraw whenever you ask, no notice
Locked until the fixed term ends

blocks.title: Balance and clearing terms
rows: The bank's policy on when funds deposited into an account can be withdrawn.
The account balance after subtracting holds, uncollected funds and any restrictions on the account.
Cash deposits, or cheques that were presented for payment and for which payment has been received.
A restriction that stops a certain part of a customer's balance from being withdrawn until an item has been collected or a specific cheque or debit has been posted.
The time of day fixed by a bank for receiving deposits. A deposit made after this time is treated as received on the next banking day.
The credit limit given to a cardholder account minus the account's present balance.
Money that has to remain in the account to qualify for special services or to waive a service charge.

blocks.title: Balance is not always available balance
blocks.text: The **ledger balance** may look high, but the **available balance** is lower once holds and uncollected funds (cheques not yet cleared) are removed. Only collected funds are really yours to withdraw.

A **cheque** is a negotiable instrument: a written order to the bank to pay a certain sum from the issuer's account to the receiver. A negotiable instrument is a document containing a promise to pay a stated amount to the intended beneficiary.

blocks.title: Cheque terms
rows: The clearing house processes the cheque; the amount is debited from the issuer's account and credited to the beneficiary's account.
A normal cheque that the bank refuses to pay, because of insufficient funds, signature mismatch or another valid reason.
The state when a depositor's account balance is too small to pay a cheque presented for payment.
A cheque written by a depositor that has not yet been presented to, or paid by, the depositor's bank.
A cheque on which the drawer's signature has been forged.
Fraudulent signing or alteration of someone else's name on an instrument such as a deed, mortgage or cheque, meant to deceive or defraud.

A cheque presented to the paying bank 180 days (6 months) or more after its issue date; the bank may return it unpaid. The maker can discourage late presentment by writing 'not good after X days' on the back.
An order not to pay a cheque that has been issued but not yet cashed. If given in time, the cheque is not debited. Most banks charge a fee for this.
A cheque drawn on a bank and signed by an authorised bank official, also called a cashier's cheque.
A process in which the cheque number, account number and bank identifier are captured and used for a one-time electronic fund transfer. The cheque itself is not the method of payment.
Imprinting MICR characters on cheques, deposits and similar items. An error in the encoded amount is an encoding error.

blocks.title: Stale-dated cheque period
blocks.text: The printed material gives 180 days (6 months) for a stale-dated cheque. In India, the validity period of a cheque is now 3 months from its date, so read the question for the figure it expects.

blocks.title: Cheque in trouble: four words
blocks.phrase: Bounced = refused; Forged = fake signature; Outstanding = not yet presented; Stale = too old.
letters: Bank refuses to pay (no funds, signature mismatch)
Written but not yet presented or paid
Presented 180 days or more after issue (as per the book)

blocks.title: Loan and credit terms
rows: Assets offered to secure a loan. If the loan is not repaid, the collateral can be seized. For a real estate mortgage, the collateral is usually the house.
A person who signs another person's note to support that person's credit and becomes responsible for the obligation.
A person who takes responsibility for the repayment of a loan. Usually the guarantor is not liable for repayment, but in some cases the responsibility does lie with the guarantor.
A form completed by an applicant giving details such as residence, employment, income and existing debt so that creditworthiness can be judged. An application fee may be charged.
An agency that collects individuals' credit information and sells it to creditors such as banks, mortgage lenders and credit card companies so they can decide on granting loans.
A detailed report of a person's credit history prepared by a credit bureau and used by lenders to judge a loan applicant.
A number, roughly between 300 and 800 as per the book, that measures a person's creditworthiness. Banks use it to decide whether you qualify for a card, loan or service.
A pre-approved loan authorisation with a borrowing limit set by creditworthiness. The borrower can take several loans without reapplying as long as the total stays within the limit.
A credit agreement, typically a credit card, allowing borrowing against a pre-approved limit. Only the amount actually borrowed plus interest is billed. Also called open-end credit or charge account.
A loan where the interest rate and payment stay the same throughout; equal monthly payments of principal and interest continue until the debt is paid.
A fee a lender charges for making the loan, in addition to interest.
The ratio of the loan principal (amount borrowed) to the appraised value (selling price) of the asset.
A debt that was not paid when due.
A fee for delinquent payment on an instalment loan, usually stated as a percentage of the balance or of the payment.
A payment postponed to a future date.
Complete repayment of a loan, including principal, interest and other dues, either over the full term or through prepayments.
A penalty on a borrower for repaying the loan before its due date.

blocks.title: Guarantor vs co-signer
blocks.text: A co-signer signs the note and becomes responsible for the obligation from the start. A guarantor usually is not liable unless the terms say so, though in some cases the repayment responsibility lies with the guarantor.

blocks.title: Credit score range
letters: Low end of the score range
High end of the score range
blocks.note: As per the book the range is roughly 300 to 800; the CIBIL scale used in India runs from 300 to 900.

blocks.title: Mortgage family
rows: A real estate related legal agreement between lender and borrower where the borrower's property serves as collateral. If installments stop, the lender has the right to take possession.
A loan made by a lender to a borrower to finance real property.
The borrower in a mortgage; the property is used as collateral.
A mortgage with a set interest rate and payments that do not change over the term of the loan.
A mortgage whose payments stay the same throughout because the interest rate and other terms are fixed.
A loan against the built-up equity in a home, i.e. the difference between its selling value and what is still owed. Often called a second mortgage; on default the bank may foreclose.
A legal process in which property that secures a loan in default can be sold to repay the loan.

blocks.title: Overdraft and related terms
rows: The excess when more money is withdrawn than is available in the account; the account is then said to be overdrawn. Some banks allow certain customers to overdraw up to a set limit.
To write a cheque for more than the amount lying in the account.
An open-end credit account whose assigned limit has been exceeded.
A bank's legal right to seize funds that a guarantor or debtor has on deposit in order to cover a loan in default.

blocks.title: Mortgagor vs Mortgagee
blocks.phrase: The mortgagOR is the One who Owes (borrower); the mortgagEE is the Eager lender who gets the security.
letters: Lender: holds the claim on the property
blocks.note: Same pattern as employer and employee: the -or acts, the -ee receives.

blocks.title: Overdraft vs overdraw
blocks.text: **Overdraw** is the act of writing a cheque for more than your balance. **Overdraft** is the resulting excess amount (the account is overdrawn). **Over limit** applies to a credit account that has crossed its limit.

blocks.title: Interest terms
rows: The cost of using money, a right, share or title in property.
The amount paid by a borrower to a lender for using the lender's money for a period. It is paid on loans or debt instruments either at regular intervals or as a lump sum at maturity.
Interest earned or accumulated on an investment but not yet paid; also called interest receivable.
An interest rate tied to a specific time period, such as a monthly or daily periodic rate (cost of credit per month or per day).
Any interest rate or dividend that changes periodically.
A rate that stays unchanged for the life of the loan.

blocks.title: Rates linked to the RBI and banks
rows: The rate at which the RBI lends funds to commercial banks, usually a long-term loan governed by the RBI's long-term monetary policy.
The rate at which a bank borrows money from the RBI by pledging or selling government securities to it.
The rate the RBI offers when banks with surplus funds deposit them with it for short periods.

The minimum interest rate of a bank below which it cannot lend, except in cases allowed by the RBI (DRI advances, loans to the bank's own employees, and loans to depositors against their own deposits).
Benchmark Prime Lending Rate. It applied normally only to loans sanctioned before the Base Rate was introduced (July 2010).

blocks.title: Repo vs Reverse Repo
blocks.phrase: REPO: banks REceive money from the RBI (RBI lends). REVERSE repo: the RBI is on the receiving end (banks park surplus).
letters: Bank borrows from the RBI against government securities
Bank deposits surplus funds with the RBI
RBI's long-term lending rate to banks
Bank's floor below which it cannot lend (with exceptions)
blocks.note: Banks borrow from the RBI at repo; they lend to the RBI at reverse repo.

blocks.title: Base Rate exceptions
blocks.text: A bank cannot lend below its Base Rate except for DRI advances, loans to its own employees and loans to its depositors against their own deposits. BPLR was the earlier benchmark, replaced by the Base Rate in July 2010.

blocks.title: Card and billing terms
rows: An account entry showing money you owe a lender, or money taken out of your deposit account.
A card that gives electronic access to the account holder's funds. It can be used at ATMs for cash or at point-of-sale terminals; the account is debited and the payee credited immediately.

Generally a four-character secret number or word given to credit or debit cardholders to access their accounts. It is assigned randomly by the bank or chosen by the customer to prevent unauthorised use.
The location where a transaction takes place, including the systems that let customers move funds from their deposit accounts at retail establishments.
The time interval between the dates on which regular periodic statements are issued.
The date on which a periodic or monthly statement is generated, after calculating finance charges, minimum payment due and the new balance.
The billing summary produced at specified intervals, usually monthly.
The date by which an instalment or loan payment is due; payments after it are late and may attract fees and penalties.
A charge made by a bank for processing transactions and maintaining accounts.
A fee charged by your bank for making a transaction at another bank's ATM.

blocks.title: Billing date vs due date
blocks.text: The **billing date** is when the statement is generated; the **payment due date** is later and is the last day to pay without a late fee. The gap between two billing dates is the **billing cycle**.

blocks.title: Electronic banking terms
rows: A machine that carries out transactions and bank services electronically using an ATM or debit card.
A service that lets an account holder get account information and carry out certain transactions through a computer using the bank's website on the Internet.
Transfer of money between accounts through electronic systems such as ATMs and electronic bill payment, rather than by cheque or cash. Wire transfers, cheques and drafts are not in this category.
An EFT authorised in advance to recur at substantially regular intervals.
A written arrangement authorising the bank to debit the customer's account to pay bills or loan instalments.

A computerised, nation-wide electronic clearing facility used to combine, sort and distribute inter-bank credits and debits. It processes direct deposits of salaries and government benefits and preauthorised transfers, and cuts manual work.

A bank's commitment, issued on behalf of a buyer or importer, to pay a seller or exporter a stated amount. The seller must meet the LoC's conditions and submit the required documents. Used mostly in large international trade deals.

blocks.title: How a Letter of Credit works
items: The buyer or importer asks its bank to issue a Letter of Credit.
The bank promises to pay the seller or exporter a stated amount.
The seller ships the goods and meets the conditions written in the LoC.
The seller submits the required documents.
On compliance, the payment is made.

blocks.title: E-banking synonyms
blocks.phrase: Internet banking = online banking = e-banking: one idea, three names.

blocks.title: Three identity codes of banking
rows: Identifies the individual bank branches that take part in online transfers such as NEFT and RTGS; printed on cheque leaves.
A numeric code that uniquely identifies a bank branch in the ECS credit scheme; printed on MICR cheques.
Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication
A standard bank identifier code used mainly for international money transfers between banks.

blocks.title: Structure of a SWIFT code
rows: Identifies the branch; an 8-character code refers to the primary office

blocks.title: SWIFT: 4-2-2-3
blocks.phrase: Big Cats Live Beyond: Bank, Country, Location, Branch.

blocks.title: Code lengths: IFSC 11, MICR 9
blocks.phrase: IFSC has 11 characters, MICR has 9 digits: 'I-F-S-C' travels online (11), 'M-I-C-R' lives on the cheque (9).
blocks.note: IFSC and the long SWIFT code are both 11 characters long: do not mix them up with the 9-digit MICR.

blocks.title: India and SWIFT
blocks.text: India was the 74th nation to join the SWIFT network. IFSC works for domestic transfers (NEFT/RTGS); SWIFT is for cross-border transfers.

blocks.title: Service terms
rows: Financial services a bank offers customers: accepting bills arising from trade, arranging and providing underwriting, managing new issues, advising on starting a business, acquisitions, mergers and foreign exchange.
Banking services offered to corporate entities, large institutions and other financial institutions.

A company that invests its clients' pooled funds into securities matching a declared financial objective, earning income through service fees. It gives investors more diversification and options. Mutual funds, hedge funds and pension plans are run by such companies.
A written instrument authorising one person to act as another's agent or attorney, for a specific act or in general. If no expiry is stated, it usually ends when the person granting it dies.

blocks.title: Wholesale vs retail
blocks.text: **Wholesale banking** deals with corporates, large institutions and other financial institutions. **Merchant banking** covers underwriting, issue management, mergers and advisory work.

blocks.title: Compliance terms
rows: Creating the appearance that large sums obtained from serious crimes, such as drug trafficking or terrorist activity, came from a legitimate source.
General Anti-Avoidance Rules: a set of general rules enacted to check tax avoidance, which is a concern worldwide.

Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority: India's pension regulator, headquartered in New Delhi, established by the Government of India on 23 August 2003. It promotes old-age income security by regulating pension funds, regulates the National Pension System (NPS) and administers the Atal Pension Yojana (APY).
Blocks or platforms such as digital identification, payment infrastructure and data exchange solutions that help countries deliver essential services and promote digital inclusion.
A unique cryptographic token that exists on a blockchain. It can digitally represent physical assets such as artwork or real estate.

blocks.title: KYC in India
items: RBI introduced Know Your Customer (KYC) guidelines for all banks.
RBI directed that banks be fully compliant with KYC provisions.
Deadline for banks to comply fully.

blocks.title: Four key elements of a bank's KYC policy
items: Customer Acceptance Policy.
Customer Identification Procedures.
Monitoring of Transactions.
Risk Management.
Main aim: prevent money laundering, terrorist financing and theft.
KYC checks include ID, face, document (for example a utility bill as address proof) and biometric verification.

blocks.title: KYC's four elements: AIM-R
blocks.phrase: KYC lets banks AIM Right: Acceptance, Identification, Monitoring, Risk.

blocks.title: Years to remember
blocks.text: KYC guidelines: **2002**. Compliance deadline: **31 December 2005**. PFRDA: **23 August 2003**, headquartered in New Delhi.
**Inflation** is a rise in the prices of goods and services in an economy over a period of time. It lowers the real value of money, so the same rupee buys less.

blocks.title: Types of inflation (as listed)
items: Wage inflation
Price power inflation
Cost-push inflation
Sectoral inflation
Stagflation
Mild inflation
Hyper-inflation

blocks.title: Effects of inflation
items: Decreases the real value of money.
Discourages investment and savings.
Leads to a shortage of goods.
Seen as a way to ease economic recessions (a mild-inflation view).
Reduces the real level of debt (a borrower's gain).

blocks.title: Seven types of inflation
blocks.phrase: Wise Pandas Count Silver Stars, Munching Honey.

blocks.title: Other terms that appear in this chapter
rows: A budgeting method where each year's budget starts from scratch rather than from last year's figures.
The maximum capital a company can raise during its lifetime; also called registered or nominal capital.
The market for buying and selling precious metals such as gold and silver.
How easily and quickly an asset can be converted into other assets.
A measure of a firm's ability to meet all its future obligations.
Bringing the fiscal deficit down to a particular level by an Act of law is a measure of fiscal reform.

blocks.title: Authorised vs paid-up capital
blocks.text: **Authorised (registered/nominal) capital** is the ceiling a company may raise in its life. **Paid-up capital** is only what shareholders have actually paid. Do not treat them as the same.

revision: Time deposit: no withdrawal before the fixed period ends; demand deposit can be withdrawn anytime.
Zero-balance account needs no minimum or average balance.
Available balance = balance minus holds, uncollected funds and restrictions.
A bounced cheque is refused for insufficient funds, signature mismatch or other valid reasons.
Stale-dated cheque as per the book: presented 180 days (6 months) or more after issue; in India validity is 3 months.
Mortgagor is the borrower; mortgagee is the lender.
Overdraft is the excess of withdrawal over the balance; right of offset lets a bank seize deposits to cover a defaulted loan.
Repo: bank borrows from the RBI against securities; reverse repo: RBI takes banks' surplus; bank rate: RBI's long-term loan rate.
Base Rate is the floor for bank lending (with RBI-allowed exceptions); BPLR applied to loans before July 2010.
IFSC has 11 characters (NEFT/RTGS); MICR has 9 digits; SWIFT has 8 or 11 characters.
SWIFT structure: 4 bank + 2 country + 2 location + optional 3 branch; India was the 74th nation to join.
KYC began in 2002; compliance deadline 31 December 2005; four elements are acceptance, identification, monitoring and risk management.
PFRDA was established on 23 August 2003, is based in New Delhi, regulates NPS and administers APY.
GAAR is General Anti-Avoidance Rules, meant to check tax avoidance.
Seven types of inflation include wage, price power, cost-push, sectoral, stagflation, mild and hyper.
